A struct is a value type and a class is a reference type; almost every other difference follows from that one.

- **struct** — copied on assignment and on every function call. No inheritance. Free memberwise initializer. Methods that change stored properties must be marked `mutating`. Small ones live on the stack or inline in their container.
- **class** — shared by reference and counted by ARC. Supports inheritance, `deinit`, and identity comparison with `===`. Always heap-allocated.

Use struct by default. Reach for class only when you need something a value cannot provide: identity that many owners must share, inheritance, `deinit` for cleanup, or `AnyObject` conformance for Objective-C interop and `weak` references.

Concurrency has sharpened the rule. A struct of Sendable properties is Sendable for free, while a class with `var` properties is not — sharing one across tasks is a compile error under the Swift 6 language mode unless you make it an actor, make it immutable, or take a lock and claim `@unchecked Sendable`.

A protocol declares a contract — methods, properties, associated types, initializers — that conforming types must implement.

### Differences vs Java/C# interfaces
- Both classes AND value types (struct, enum) can conform.
- Protocols can have associated types — generic-like type parameters (`associatedtype Item`).
- Protocol extensions can provide default implementations and add methods to all conformers without modifying their source.
- Existentials (`any Protocol`) are runtime-erased boxes; opaque types (`some Protocol`) are compile-time concrete.

Protocol-oriented programming (POP) is Swift's idiomatic answer to inheritance.

A Swift enum is a full type that can carry data, which is why it models a closed set of alternatives far better than a set of integer constants.

- **Raw values** — every case maps to the same underlying primitive (Int, String, Character). The compiler synthesises `RawRepresentable`, giving you `HTTPStatus(rawValue: 404)` and `.ok.rawValue`. Note the initializer is failable, because an unknown raw value has no case.
- **Associated values** — each case carries its own typed payload, and different cases can carry different payloads. That is what makes an enum an algebraic data type, and it is the right shape for screen state, parser tokens, and anything with a "loading / loaded / failed" life.

A case can have raw values or associated values, never both.

Enums are value types and can carry methods, computed properties, static members and protocol conformances just like a struct. Pair them with `switch`, which the compiler checks for exhaustiveness — add a case and every switch that forgot it fails to compile, which is the whole point.

`indirect` allows recursive cases (a tree, a linked list) by boxing the payload behind a pointer.

Extensions add functionality to an existing type — your own types, standard library types, even types imported from a framework — without subclassing and without touching the original source.

### Can add
- Computed properties (instance and static)
- Methods (instance, static, and `mutating`)
- Initializers (convenience initializers for classes)
- Subscripts
- Protocol conformance, including conditional conformance
- Nested types

### Cannot add
- **Stored properties** — there is no room for them in the original type's memory layout
- **Overrides of existing methods** — an extension adds, it never replaces
- A designated initializer on a class you do not own

One Swift 6 wrinkle: conforming an imported type to an imported protocol (`extension URL: Identifiable`) is a retroactive conformance, and the compiler now warns about it, because the owning module could add the same conformance later and the two would collide. Spell it `extension URL: @retroactive Identifiable` to acknowledge the risk, or wrap the type instead.

Idiomatic uses: split a large type into feature-sized chunks, conform a type you do not own to a protocol you do own, add helpers to Array and String, and keep protocol default implementations out of the protocol declaration.

Protocol-oriented programming (POP) — a Swift idiom championed at WWDC 2015 — composes behavior via small protocols and default implementations rather than deep class hierarchies.

### Why POP over class inheritance
- Works with structs and enums, not just classes
- **Multiple conformance** — a type can adopt many protocols, sidestepping single-inheritance
- **Composition over inheritance** — features added in tiny chunks (`Equatable`, `Hashable`, `Identifiable`) and mixed at will
- **Better testability** — protocols become natural mock boundaries
- No fragile-base-class problem

When to keep inheritance: deep frameworks (`UIView`/`NSObject`), Cocoa/UIKit interop, override-based template methods.

Swift has six access levels, and a member is always capped by the visibility of the type that contains it.

### From most to least visible
- **open** — visible everywhere AND subclassable/overridable from another module. Classes and their members only.
- **public** — visible from any module, but subclassing and overriding are limited to the defining module.
- **package** — visible from any target in the same Swift package. Fills the gap between `internal` and `public` for multi-module packages.
- internal (the default) — visible inside the current module only.
- **fileprivate** — visible inside the same source file.
- **private** — visible inside the enclosing declaration and its extensions in the same file.

The containment rule catches people out: a `public` method on an `internal` type is effectively internal, and a `public` function cannot expose an `internal` type in its signature. Initializers default to `internal`, which is why a `public struct` from a package is not constructible from outside until you write `public init`.

Start closed and widen deliberately. `private` by default keeps the invariants of a type inside the type, and a small `public` surface is the only thing that makes a module's API reviewable.

Swift lets a stored property carry behaviour in two ways: observers that fire around a change, and `lazy`, which defers the initializer until the first read.

- **willSet / didSet** — run just before and just after the value changes. `willSet` sees `newValue`, `didSet` sees `oldValue`. They only apply to stored properties, and they do NOT fire when you assign from inside the type's own initializer.
- **lazy** — the initializer runs on first access, not at init time. It must be a `var` (the storage is written on first read), it can refer to `self`, and it is not thread-safe: two concurrent first-reads can run the initializer twice.
- **Computed property** — no storage at all; the getter runs on every access and an optional setter runs on every assignment.

Pick by intent: observers for side effects on change (invalidate a layout, fire analytics), `lazy` for an expensive default you may never need, computed for a value that is always derivable from other state.

Two traps worth remembering. Observers fire on every assignment, even when the new value equals the old one, so guard with `oldValue` when the work is expensive. And a `lazy` property is a mutation, so reading one on a `let` struct instance will not compile.

Swift will not let you touch self until every stored property in the whole inheritance chain has a value, and the designated versus convenience split is the rule system that guarantees it.

### The two kinds of initializer
- A designated initializer fully initializes its own class: it gives every stored property the class declares a value, and then calls a designated initializer of its superclass. Designated initializers delegate up.
- A convenience initializer is marked `convenience` and must call another initializer in the same class, eventually landing on a designated one. Convenience initializers delegate across.

### The two phases in order
1. Bottom-up, every stored property from this class up to the root gets an initial value. Nothing may read self, call an instance method, or use an inherited property during this phase — that is what the "self used before all stored properties are initialized" error is telling you.
2. Once the chain is complete, initialization walks back down and each initializer may customize: call methods, set inherited properties, hand self to something else.

The inheritance rules that surprise people: a subclass inherits no initializers at all by default. It inherits every designated initializer of its superclass if it declares no designated initializer of its own, and it inherits the convenience ones once it has implemented all of the superclass's designated initializers. `required` forces every subclass to provide the initializer, which is why UIKit subclasses keep re-declaring the coder-based one.

Two more forms worth naming: a failable `init?` returns nil for input it cannot accept, and structs get a memberwise initializer for free — internal by default, so a public struct in a package needs an explicit public one written by hand.

It has to conform to Hashable, which means being Equatable as well and hashing in a way that agrees with equality.

The contract is one sentence with real consequences: if two values are equal they must produce the same hash. Collisions in the other direction are fine and expected. Break the rule and nothing crashes — lookups just silently miss, which is the nastiest bug in this area. The two usual ways to break it are hashing a field that `==` ignores, and mutating a value after using it as a key.

### What you get for free
- A struct becomes Equatable and Hashable by declaring the conformance, as long as every stored property already conforms. The compiler writes `==` and `hash(into:)` over all stored properties.
- An enum with no payloads is Hashable outright; one with payloads is as soon as the payloads are.
- Classes get nothing synthesized. Write both by hand, and be careful with subclasses — comparing types inside `==`, or marking the class `final`, avoids the asymmetric-equality trap.

Two neighbours often confused with it. `Comparable` is what sorting needs: implement `<` and the rest of the operators come from the standard library. `Identifiable` is not about equality at all — it gives SwiftUI a stable id for diffing, and two values with the same id can legitimately differ.

For classes, remember that `==` is the equality you define, while `===` asks whether two references point at the same instance.

Because the delegate normally owns the object that calls it, so a strong reference back would close a cycle and leak both sides forever.

The shape is always the same: a view controller owns a table view, and the table view's delegate is that same view controller. If the delegate reference is strong, the two hold each other, ARC never reaches zero, and neither is deallocated. A weak reference breaks the loop and becomes nil automatically when the owner goes away, which is why the property is an optional.

For `weak` to be legal the reference must be to a class instance, so the protocol has to be class-bound — declare it as inheriting from AnyObject. Without that a struct could conform, and a weak reference to a value type is meaningless and does not compile.

### A few things worth knowing around it
- Optional requirements need an Objective-C protocol and an NSObject-based conformer. In pure Swift, give the protocol a default implementation in an extension instead and let conformers ignore what they do not care about.
- Name the callbacks after what happened, and pass the sender back — that is the convention UIKit uses so one object can be the delegate of several sources.
- A closure property is the better tool for a single callback, but it captures strongly, so the closure's body needs a weak capture of self for exactly the same reason.
- Under strict concurrency, mark the protocol as main-actor bound when its callbacks touch UI, so a background caller is a compile error rather than a rare glitch.

Modern alternatives: async/await for a one-shot result, AsyncStream for a sequence of events, and a delegate when the contract is several related callbacks.

It depends on the type the compiler sees at the call site, because a method that is not a protocol requirement is dispatched statically rather than through the conformance.

### Two different mechanisms are at work
- A method declared in the protocol body is a requirement. It gets a slot in the type's witness table, so a call always goes through that slot and lands on the conforming type's implementation, no matter what static type the value is held as. The extension version is then only a default for types that do not supply one.
- A method that appears only in the extension has no slot. The compiler resolves it from the static type: through a variable typed as the protocol you get the extension's version, through a variable typed as the concrete type you get the type's own. The same object, two answers.

That is not a bug, it is the cost of default implementations being ordinary functions. The rule that avoids it: anything you intend conformers to customize belongs in the protocol body, and the extension supplies the default.

The same static-versus-dynamic question turns up elsewhere in Swift, and interviewers often chain it:
- Class methods go through a vtable, so subclasses override normally; marking a class or method `final`, or making it private, restores static dispatch and lets the optimizer inline.
- Structs and enums have no inheritance, so their methods are always statically dispatched.
- `@objc dynamic` opts a member into Objective-C message dispatch, which is what KVO and method swizzling need.

A `class` member can be overridden by a subclass and a `static` member cannot — static is simply the final form of a type-level declaration.

### Details that matter in practice
- `static func` and `static var` exist on structs, enums, classes and protocols. They belong to the type, not to an instance, and no subclass can replace them.
- `class func` and computed `class var` exist only on classes, and a subclass may redeclare them with `override`. Stored type properties must be static — a class cannot declare a stored `class var`.
- `final` on a class forbids subclassing; on a method or property it forbids overriding. Beyond intent, it lets the compiler replace vtable dispatch with a direct call and inline across it, which is one of the cheapest optimizations available in Swift.
- A protocol writes its type-level requirements with `static`. A class satisfies one with `class` when it wants subclasses to override it, or with `static` when it does not.

The idiomatic singleton is `static let shared`, and it is safe: type properties are initialized lazily, exactly once, even under concurrent access.

Strict concurrency has sharpened all of this. A mutable `static var` is global mutable state that any task can touch, so the Swift 6 language mode rejects it. The ways out are to make it a `let` of a Sendable type, isolate it to a global actor such as the main actor, or wrap the state in an actor. `nonisolated(unsafe)` exists for the cases you have protected some other way, and it is a promise the compiler cannot check.
